question: Identify an anomaly element that belongs to both group 1 and group 17.
solution:
correct answer is __**Hydrogen.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hydrogen **exhibits unique properties that allow it to be considered for placement in **both Group 1 and Group 17 **of the periodic table.
 
• In some aspects, hydrogen resembles **alkali metals** found in Group 1, such as its ability to easily form cations. This characteristic aligns with the behavior of alkali metals.
 
• Hydrogen also shares properties with halogens found in Group 17. For example, it forms H2, which is a true property of halogens.
 
• Hydrogen can both accept and donate electrons to achieve stability, a trait shared with elements in both groups.
 
• As the smallest member of its family, hydrogen's unique properties make its classification in the periodic table intriguing and subject to debate.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydrogen** shares several properties with both Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 17 (halogens) elements:
 
• **Similarities to Group 1 (Alkali Metals):**
 
 
• Like alkali metals, hydrogen has one electron in its outermost shell.
 
• For example, hydrogen (H-1), lithium (Li-2,1), sodium (Na+), and potassium (K+). Hydrogen can lose its outermost electron to form a hydrogen ion (H+), similar to how alkali metals form ions such as Na+ and K+.
 
• Hydrogen can combine with non-metals like oxygen and sulfur to form oxides and sulfides, akin to how alkali metals react with non-metals.
 
• Hydrogen acts as a strong reducing agent, much like alkali metals do in chemical reactions.
 
 
 
• **Similarities to Group 17 (Halogens):**
 
 
• Halogens have a strong tendency to gain one electron to form halide ions.
 
• Similarly, hydrogen exhibits some tendency to gain one electron to form a hydride ion. Hydrogen, like halogens, can have an oxidation state of -1.
 
• Hydrogen readily combines with non-metals such as carbon, silicon, and nitrogen to form covalent compounds, resembling the reactivity of halogens with non-metals.
